newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire army hits back in east, curfew in Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army hits back in east, curfew in Kisangani.

text.p: William Wallis
Zaire's government said on Monday that its army had launched a counter-attack against rebels in the east but the rebel leader in the eastern town of Goma said the Zairean troops had been pushed back.
"The counter-attack certainly took place," Koloni Longo, spokesman of Zaire's new crisis government, told Reuters. He declined further details.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said earlier in the captured city of Goma that the rebels had beaten back the attack, launched late on Sunday in the Uvira region to the south.

Kabila, who heads the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), said his forces had captured many weapons and dead bodies abandoned by the fleeing army but there was no independent confirmation.
Earlier, the governor of Upper Zaire, on the fringe of the initial conflict zone but increasingly affected, declared a curfew in the provinicial capital Kisangani.

Zaire's president, Mobutu Sese Seko, returned from four months cancer treatment and rest in Europe on December 17. He reshuffled the government and named a new army chief to end the revolt in the east.

But the rebels have thrust out from the North and South Kivu area they originally controlled. Fighting has most recently raged around the eastern town of Bunia in Upper Zaire. The alliance that began the rebellion three months ago with a group of mostly ethnic Tutsis, now occupies a 500 km (300 mile) swath of eastern Zaire along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
Koloni said on Monday fighting was continuing around Bunia. "You can rest assured that it will continue until not one grain of Zairean territory will remain in the hands of the others."
Bunia is on the threshold of vast gold and mineral resources in the Upper Zaire province, and was one of the few remaining airstrips in the east used by the army to bring reinforcements.
It is also at the head of one of the few passable roads in the region west to Kisangani, the biggest city in the east, in the heart of the jungle and which the rebels have threatened to target.

Upper Zaire governor Lombeya Bosongo told state television earlier that a curfew was imposed on Kisangani. The television said the curfew would run from 7 p.m. to 6 a.m., adding it was designed to control potential infiltrations by rebels.
Kisangani is around 600 km (400 miles) from Bunia in the heart of the tropical jungle. The Tutsi-led rebels have threatened on numerous occasions to target the town.

A local official in Upper Zaire in contact with several towns by radio from Kinshasa said fighting was taking place at Nia Nia and Bafwasende, between 200 and 250 km (120 to 160 miles) northeast of Kisangani, and that rebels were advancing up the road from Walikale, around 350 km (220 miles) to the southeast.
The governor, contacted by telephone at his Kisangani headquarters, dismissed the reports as rumours.
Reports from north of Kisangani say several hundred soldiers mutineed in Isiro, looting shops and businesses and killing a German priest and other people before heading west.

The local official from the region said the mutinous troops had taken trucks and pillaged their way along the road to Buta, 600 km (370 miles) west of Bunia, causing the population of the town to flee into the bush.
Both the government spokesman in Kinshasa and the governor of Upper Zaire confirmed there had been problems in Isiro but were reserved about the extent. Koloni said rebels may have been to blame.
Mobutu left Kinshasa on Sunday for his Gbadolite jungle palace. His spokesman told Reuters he would return in 10 days.
Africa's latest conflict was sparked off by Zairean attempts to expel back to Rwanda the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group that migrated to the area now known as Zaire up to 200 years ago.
The Banyamulenge, backed by Rwanda's battle-hardened Tutsi-dominated army, resisted and took up arms to fight for their rights as Zaireans.
